title: Review lifecycle replay with claim expiry and escalation
scenario: An out-of-order event log is replayed through a labeling/review state machine with role checks, review-claim expiry, rework escalation and a final as_of sweep. Test 3 covers the review queue (paused projects excluded) and cycle times.

verified.why_correct: Sending a reject back to LABELING instead of a 'rejected' state looks odd, but it is exactly the README table. The escalation compares the rework count *after* this reject with max_rework, so the second reject escalates when max_rework is 2.
-priority looks like a flipped sort, but the README says the higher number is more urgent, so negating it puts the most urgent first. Oldest created first and then task id match the spec.

bugs.title: Claim treated as expired at its deadline
bugs.symptom: Test 1 test_final_states: T-10 ends as 'submitted' instead of 'in_review'. Nothing else changes, not even the queue, because T-10's project (beta) is paused.
bugs.why: T-10 was claimed at 16:30 with a 90-minute TTL, so its deadline is exactly as_of (18:00). The spec says an action exactly at the deadline is still in time, but `>=` releases the claim in the final sweep.
hints: Only T-10 has the wrong final state. Work out its claim deadline and compare it with as_of.
Look at the expiry comparison used by the replay and the final sweep.
probes: T-10 now ends in submitted. Why doesn't it show up in the queue?
Which other event in the log would also have changed if it had landed exactly on a deadline?

bugs.title: Duplicate key uses the raw actor id
bugs.symptom: Test 1 test_violations: an extra first entry `{'line': 8, 'task': 'T-01', 'action': 'approve', 'reason': 'invalid transition'}`. States, rework and reviewer counts are unchanged.
bugs.why: Line 8 repeats line 7's approve with actor `RV-01`. The dedupe key keeps the raw case, so the copy survives. Replaying it on an already-approved task adds an `invalid transition` violation, while the task itself and the stats are unchanged.
hints: Look at the extra violation's line in events.csv and the line just above it.
How does load_events decide that two rows are the same event?
Build the key from the normalised `actor`, not clean(row["actor"]).
probes: Why didn't the duplicate approve change T-01's state or rv-01's counts?
If the duplicate had been a claim_review, would anything besides violations have changed?

bugs.title: `or` makes every decision count as approved
bugs.symptom: Test 2 test_reviewer_decisions: rv-02 shows approved 1 / rejected 0 (should be 0 / 1) and rv-03 approved 2 / rejected 0 (should be 0 / 2). Claims are correct.
bugs.why: `t.action == "approve" or "resolve"` parses as `(t.action == "approve") or "resolve"`, and the non-empty string is always truthy. Every non-claim transition, rejects included, lands in `approved`.
hints: rv-02 and rv-03 show approvals but no rejections. Check the log: did they ever approve?
Look at how reviewer_decisions classifies each transition.
probes: Why were the claims counts still right?
How would a linter or a quick REPL check catch this kind of expression?

bugs.title: Review samples stored on the class
bugs.old:
samples: list

    def __init__(self, reviewer):
        self.reviewer = reviewer
        self.samples = []
bugs.symptom: Test 2 test_review_minutes: `{'rv-01': 31.0, 'rv-02': 31.0, 'rv-03': 31.0} != {'rv-01': 37.5, 'rv-02': 30.0, 'rv-03': 25.0}`. Every reviewer gets the same mean.
bugs.why: With `samples = []` at class level and no per-instance list, every ReviewTimer appends to the same list. Each reviewer's mean is then the mean over all decisions (31.0).
hints: Every reviewer has the same mean. What would make their samples identical?
Look at where ReviewTimer keeps its samples.
Create the list per instance: `self.samples = []` in __init__.
probes: Why does `self.samples.append(...)` change a class attribute, while `self.samples = [...]` wouldn't?
Would building a fresh list in __init__ ever share state between timers?

bugs.title: Removing paused tasks while iterating the queue
bugs.symptom: Test 3 test_queue: `['T-07', 'T-08', 'T-09', 'T-04', 'T-05', 'T-11']`. T-07 (paused project delta) is still at the front.
bugs.why: Removing T-06 shifts T-07 into the slot the loop has already passed, so the loop never looks at T-07 and the paused delta task stays in the queue.
hints: T-07 is in a paused project but still in the queue, while T-06 (also paused) is gone. Where do they sit in the sorted list?
Look at how build_queue drops paused tasks.
Iterate over a copy (`list(queue)`) or build a new filtered list.
probes: Why was T-06 removed but not T-07?
Would the problem show up if the two paused tasks weren't next to each other?

bugs.title: Cycle time uses timedelta.seconds
bugs.symptom: Test 3 test_cycle_hours: T-02 shows 3.0 instead of 27.0; T-01 and T-03 are correct.
bugs.why: timedelta.seconds is only the seconds part after whole days are taken out. T-02 took 1 day 3 hours, so `.seconds` gives 3 hours. The other tasks took less than a day and look correct.
hints: Only T-02 is off, by exactly 24 hours. What is special about it?
Look at how cycle_hours turns the timedelta into a number.
probes: What does timedelta(days=1, hours=3).seconds return, and why?
Why did review_minutes not have the same problem?

context_qa.q: What does replay() do for each event, in order?
context_qa.a: It sorts events by (ts, line). For each one it looks up the task (unknown → violation), calls _release_if_expired with the event time, checks actor_allowed, asks next_state for the target, checks the claim holder for approve/reject, then records a Transition and updates the task. After the loop it calls _release_if_expired on every task with settings['as_of'].

context_qa.q: What does a Transition record, and where is claim_at taken from?
context_qa.a: ts, task_id, actor, action, and claim_at, which is the task's claim_at at the moment the event is applied. For approve/reject that is the time of the claim_review being decided; for other actions it is usually None.

context_qa.q: How does load_events treat duplicate rows?
context_qa.a: It keeps a `seen` set of keys and skips any row whose key is already in it, so the first copy is kept. Line numbers come from enumerate(..., start=2), since the header is line 1.

context_qa.q: Which tasks have open review claims near the end of the log?
context_qa.a: T-10 (claimed by rv-02 at 2026-06-12 16:30) and T-12 (claimed by rv-03 at 17:00). With claim_ttl_minutes = 90, their deadlines are 18:00 and 18:30; as_of is 2026-06-12 18:00.

context_qa.q: How does build_queue order and filter tasks?
context_qa.a: It sorts every task in State.SUBMITTED by priority_key, then removes tasks whose project is in settings['paused'] (beta and delta in this data), and returns the ids.

For each approve/reject transition that has claim_at, it gets or creates a ReviewTimer for the actor (dict.setdefault) and adds (ts - claim_at) in minutes. Each reviewer's value is ReviewTimer.mean(), rounded to 1 decimal.

context_qa.q: Is State a str enum? How are states compared?
context_qa.a: State is a plain enum.Enum with lower-case string values. The code compares with `is` (e.g. task.state is State.IN_REVIEW), and the report outputs state.value.
